extraction.research_question: Can audio be made usable as data for political research, given the "alignment crisis" (large text and audio corpora that do not intersect at the utterance level), and which audio features (LLDs, MFCCs, learned embeddings) and classifiers are useful for speech characterization, speaker identification, and emotion/valence measurement? The paper is a methods-and-applications demonstration; it does not test a substantive hypothesis.
extraction.theory: No formal theory is tested. The framing draws on the text-as-data literature (Grimmer and Stewart 2013; Wilkerson and Casas 2017) and on the claim that nonverbal audio cues (pitch, energy, intonation) carry political meaning not captured by transcripts (Section 2; Klofstad 2016; Dietrich et al. 2019; Damann, Knox and Lucas 2025). Emotion is treated as socially and politically constructed (Section 4.4, p.325), so classifier outputs are framed as starting points, not measures of emotion.
extraction.data: Unit: utterance/sentence within televised U.S. presidential and vice-presidential debates. Period: 1960 to 2020 (first televised debate 1960; 2020 included). Videos: 45 (243,023 s = 4,050 min = 67.5 h). Transcripts: 47,150 sentences (38,649 from candidates; 8,501 from moderators, panelists, or audience), originally from the USElecDeb60To16 dataset (Haddadan, Cabrio and Villata 2020), taken from the Commission on Presidential Debates site and extended to 2020, with some sentence omissions fixed (Section 4, p.317). Participants: 34 candidates (16 Democrat, 15 Republican, 3 independent), 82 moderators/panelists, 59 audience members. Video source: Commission on Presidential Debates YouTube channel. Note for the record: the speaker-identification section (Section 4.3, p.321) reports 44,559 sentences and 156 speakers, which does not reconcile with the 47,150 sentence count in Section 1 (p.314); the paper does not explain the gap. Forced-alignment validation used a random subset of 500 utterances, each rated five times by crowd annotators (p.318). Emotion models were applied to the debates; their training corpora were IEMOCAP (about 12 h of acted and improvised audio, Busso et al. 2008) and MSP-Podcast v1.7 (about 84 h, Lotfian and Busso 2019).
extraction.method: Four applications of increasing complexity (Section 4, Table 2). (1) Forced alignment: aeneas, which matches MFCCs of the audio to synthetic-voice MFCCs via dynamic time warping; validated by human ratings on a 1-5 scale. (2) Speech characterization: pYIN pitch (F0) in 32 ms rolling windows and RMS energy per utterance, normalized by each debate's average loudness; within-speaker pitch deviations averaged over 5 s windows (Figure 3c). (3) Speaker identification: a custom CNN on MFCCs (two blocks of convolution, max-pooling and dropout) versus a single-layer neural network on 768-dimensional wav2vec2-base embeddings (Hugging Face facebook/wav2vec2-base); Adam, learning rate 0.001, cross-entropy loss, batch 32 (MFCC) or 8 (wav2vec2), early stopping with patience 3 (footnote 9). (4) Emotion: off-the-shelf models, not retrained: a SpeechBrain wav2vec2 model fine-tuned on IEMOCAP for four classes (anger, happiness, sadness, neutral), and Wagner et al. (2023) dimensional models for arousal, dominance and valence trained on MSP-Podcast. Text-based emotion and sentiment classifiers are compared with audio-based labels as a cross-check (Figure 4d).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is a measurement and feasibility paper. Validation is by human crowd ratings for alignment (Section 4.1), held-out test accuracy for speaker identification (Table 3), and reported third-party benchmark accuracy/CCC for emotion models (Section 4.4). The paper explicitly says cross-speaker comparisons are confounded by microphone placement, compression, and sampling (p.320), and recommends within-speaker shifts or speaker-dependent human validation (p.324).
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. presidential and vice-presidential general-election debates, 1960-2020, all televised debate audio available on the CPD YouTube channel. Institution: candidate-moderator debate format, not legislatures. The paper argues the LLD and MFCC features are language-agnostic, but wav2vec2 embeddings and the emotion models are trained on specific languages and corpora and may not generalize across languages, accents, or cultures (Sections 3.3 and 5, pp.316, 326). Alignment and ASR context also draws on parliamentary data (UK Hansard/ParliamentTV, German Bundestag work) only in the literature review.

key_findings.finding: MFCC-based forced alignment of audio to transcripts performs well on crowd ratings; about 5% of text-audio pairs were rated not aligned at all, and short or interrupted sentences drove the poor alignment.
key_findings.numbers: 500 utterances, 5 annotations each; percentage agreement (PA) 85.26%; distance-based agreement (DA) 95.76%; about 5% rated 1 (not aligned at all).

key_findings.finding: Pitch extraction ranks candidates by average F0. Women candidates (Palin, Harris, Clinton) appear among the top five; the bottom five include Reagan, Lieberman, Edwards, Cheney and Dole. Pitch-based comparisons are presented as exploratory and confounded by recording conditions.
key_findings.numbers: 34 candidates; top five by average pitch include three of the four women candidates in the sample (Ferraro ranked sixth).

key_findings.finding: Normalized energy differs most across the two debates involving women candidates. Palin and Ferraro had lower average energy than their opponents (Biden, H.W. Bush).
key_findings.numbers: Energy normalized by each debate's average loudness; largest energy gaps appear in the Palin-Biden and Ferraro-Bush debates (no effect size reported).

key_findings.finding: Within-speaker pitch variation is far higher in 2020 than in the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debate, which the authors link to changing norms and technology but do not test.
key_findings.numbers: Comparison of 1960 and 2020 first debates, normalized to each speaker's own baseline, averaged over 5-s windows; no statistic reported.

key_findings.finding: Wav2vec2 embeddings substantially outperform MFCCs for speaker identification, and the gap widens as the number of speaker classes grows.
key_findings.numbers: Individual debates: MFCC 0.888 (+/-0.085) vs wav2vec2 0.974 (+/-0.024). All 156 speakers: MFCC 0.081 vs wav2vec2 0.914 (table 0.08103 vs 0.913568). Candidates only, 34 labels: MFCC 0.134 vs wav2vec2 0.946.

key_findings.finding: Off-the-shelf emotion models label a large share of utterances as angry, with most of the rest neutral; sad and happy are rare. The authors say the four-label scheme is too simple.
key_findings.numbers: Reported IEMOCAP four-class test accuracy of 75.3%; no per-debate figures given in text beyond the plotted percentages.

key_findings.finding: Candidates with higher pitch (Clinton, Kemp) also score as more angry, and low-pitch candidates (Cheney, Lieberman) score as calmer. The paper says these contradict expert coding of Trump, who is not among the top angry candidates in the model output.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, p.323, Figure 4b; contradiction cites Bucy et al. 2020
key_findings.numbers: Bucy et al. (2020) expert coding of the 2016 Trump-Clinton debate: Trump anger/threatening tone 82.6% of interventions vs Clinton 35.3%.

key_findings.finding: Dominance-arousal profiles place Clinton, Perot and Anderson at high dominance and high arousal; Lieberman and Cheney are lowest on both. No candidate stands out on valence.
key_findings.numbers: Model CCC for arousal 0.744, dominance 0.655, valence 0.638 (reported for the Wagner et al. 2023 model on MSP-Podcast, p.323).

key_findings.finding: Audio-based emotion labels and text-based labels only partly agree. Text emotion models mostly output neutral, while the audio model is more differentiated. Anger co-occurs with negative sentiment in 32% of cases.
key_findings.numbers: Anger-negative sentiment co-occurrence 32% (as reported in text).

limitations: Forced alignment is poor for very short or interrupted sentences (Figure 2b; p.318).

Cross-speaker and cross-time comparisons of pitch and energy are confounded by microphone placement, audio compression, sampling, and recording technology (pp.319-320, 324). The paper explicitly warns against naive interpretation.
Emotion and valence outputs are not validated against human coding of these debates; the authors call for speaker-dependent human validation (p.324).
Emotion classifiers can encode and amplify gender, ethnicity and vocal bias, possibly labeling women as angry when using neutral or assertive tones (pp.324-325).
Four-label emotion categories are simplistic (p.324). Emotion definitions vary across individuals, circumstances and cultures (p.322).
Training corpora (IEMOCAP, MSP-Podcast) are not debates; out-of-domain generalization is assumed from reported benchmarks, not tested here (p.322).
Embeddings are language-specific and computationally expensive for typical researchers; MFCC/LLD features are language-agnostic but less accurate for complex tasks (pp.316, 326).
Only U.S. presidential and VP debates are studied; the authors note the need for comparative work outside the U.S. (p.322).
Copyright prevents sharing the videos; broadcasters gave contradictory answers on rights, and CBS quoted a licensing fee from $2,500 (footnote 4, p.314).
Data-protection and copyright concerns apply when audio is sent to external ASR APIs such as Google or YouTube (p.314, footnote 2).
Sentence count does not reconcile between Section 1 (47,150) and Section 4.3 (44,559); the paper does not explain the difference (pp.314, 321).
Reported ASR error rates (WER 0.03-0.26) come from prior lab-condition validations that do not account for noise or crosstalk (Proksch, Wratil and Wackerle 2019; p.314).
measures: Word error rate (WER) and match error rate (MER) (background, footnotes 1 and 3; cited figures from prior work)
Percentage agreement (PA) and distance-based agreement (DA) for alignment ratings (Supplementary Appendix D)
Pitch F0 via pYIN, 32 ms rolling windows (p.319)
Root-mean-squared energy, normalized by debate average loudness (p.319)
Classification test accuracy for speaker identification (Table 3)
Discrete emotion label percentages (angry, happy, neutral, sad) per debate and per candidate (Figure 4a-b)
Dominance, arousal and valence scores; concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) for model benchmarks (pp.322-323)
Co-occurrence matrices between audio emotion and text emotion/sentiment labels (Figure 4d)

summary_md:
Mestre and Ryan (Political Analysis 2026) is a methods paper on audio as data. Its corpus is 45 U.S. presidential and VP debate videos (1960-2020; 47,150 transcript sentences). It runs four demonstrations. (1) Aeneas MFCC/DTW forced alignment, rated by crowd workers on 500 utterances x 5 ratings: percentage agreement 85.26%, distance agreement 95.76%, and about 5% of pairs not aligned at all, mostly short or interrupted sentences. (2) pYIN pitch and RMS energy. Energy is normalized by each debate's loudness, and within-speaker pitch deviation is shown over time. (3) Closed-set speaker identification. A single layer on mean-pooled wav2vec2-base embeddings reaches 0.914 accuracy across 156 speakers; a CNN on MFCCs reaches 0.081. (4) Off-the-shelf emotion models. The authors say these are biased by gender and pitch, and they disagree with expert coding.

For Melange the paper is less outside evidence than a method source. The speaker-identity research layer already copies it closely: `b5_audio_neural_head.py` reproduces the wav2vec2/Adam/batch-8/patience-3 head and cites section 4.3 and footnote 9, and `b5_audio_align_turns.py` uses Aeneas as the paper does. Melange's run of that same method on congressional audio failed. The fresh-21 neural EER was .226, against a bar of 5% or less. That run split train and test by source and event and used weak caption labels. The paper's 0.914 is in-domain debate audio, where the authors themselves warn that microphone placement and compression confound comparisons across speakers. So the paper's accuracy is not a benchmark Melange should expect to reach. The paper also backs the within-speaker pitch design and the fix for the sex confound in pitch variability. It cautions against the cross-member pooled eGeMAPS z-scores, which have no per-recording loudness or channel control. Its warnings about emotion models support keeping audio display-only.

gaps_exposed: Melange has no human-rated alignment validation. The paper shows a cheap protocol: 500 utterances x 5 crowd ratings, reported as PA/DA. Melange's ALIGN_MIN_TURN_WORD_MATCH 0.80 and ALIGN_MIN_HEARING_WORD_MATCH 0.70 (fec/audio_rules.py:38-39) are still uncalibrated assertions, and the 150-clip annotation packet was never coded.

The member eGeMAPS cache (fec/members/b5_audio_build.py:85-100) has no per-recording loudness or channel normalization. The paper normalizes energy by each debate's average loudness before any cross-speaker comparison.

The cause of the transfer failure is undiagnosed. The paper's wav2vec2 recipe gave 0.914 on in-domain debates and EER .226 on Melange's event-disjoint split. No experiment yet separates channel leakage from weak labels or venue mismatch. Training and testing within one venue/channel would separate them, but that would be a new look and needs Paul's go.

Melange has no audio emotion layer. If one is ever proposed, the paper's evidence requires speaker-dependent human validation and a check for gender and pitch bias first. High-pitch candidates scored as more angry, and the model disagreed with Bucy et al.'s expert coding (Trump anger in 82.6% of interventions vs Clinton 35.3%).
flags: Do not quote the paper's 0.914 (156 speakers) or 0.946 (34 candidates) wav2vec2 accuracy as what Melange should expect. The paper measures closed-set identification within one broadcast series; Melange measures event-disjoint verification. On Melange's own fresh-21 cohort the same recipe failed at EER .226.

Paul's position table lists 'No annotated literature' for melange-audio-speech.identity-two-check-design. The code (b5_audio_neural_head.py:4, b5_audio_neural_pilot.py:225) and the brain single-look cases 2-3 note both cite Mestre & Ryan 2026 as the method source, so the table is stale.

The paper's internal counts do not reconcile: Section 1 gives 47,150 sentences, and the speaker-ID section gives 44,559 sentences and 156 speakers. Name the denominator whenever the speaker-ID figures are quoted.

extraction.coverage: Full text read: all joined text lines of the PDF (33 pages in manifest; text pp.1-32 plus references). Figure 1-5 glyph matrices (text-extraction noise) were skipped; their captions and in-figure accuracy labels were read. Appendix is referenced (footnotes 9, 15) but not included in the file. extraction.research_question: Can a "minimally-supervised" sentiment dictionary built from the corpus itself (seed words plus GloVe word-vector similarity) yield valid sentiment measures for specialized vocabularies where standard dictionaries (LIWC, AFINN) fail? The paper then applies the method to U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions to measure tone across 1792-2010, including over time and per justice.
extraction.theory: Distributional hypothesis: words used in similar contexts have similar meanings (p.4-5). Word vectors trained on a domain corpus place sentiment-laden words near seed words, so a small seed set grows a domain-appropriate dictionary. Standard dictionaries embed fixed valences that may be wrong in specialized contexts (e.g., "love" and "bagel" in tennis, p.3-4). Semantic drift over time is handled by re-estimating dictionaries on temporal subsets (p.19-20). The paper argues sentiment in court opinions is a substantive proxy for justices' disagreement and the norm of consensus (p.17-18).
extraction.data: Movie reviews (benchmark): Large Movie Review Dataset, 100,000 IMDB reviews (25,000 positive, 25,000 negative, 50,000 unlabeled). Word vectors were trained on 75,000 documents (12,500 positive, 12,500 negative, 50,000 unlabeled); 25,000 held-out test documents were used for an out-of-sample check (p.9-11). Mean review length 184 tokens, max 2,085 (p.13). Supreme Court: all cases 1792-2010 from justia.com, split into opinion-level files; only majority opinions retained; matched to the Supreme Court Database (Spaeth et al. 2012). About 26,000 unique majority opinions spanning 217 years (p.18-19). Mean majority opinion length 2,097 tokens. Justice-level analyses cover justices with more than 50 majority opinions; the text cites 84 justices (p.23). Unit of analysis: document (review or majority opinion), aggregated to justice-level means.
extraction.method: Minimally-supervised dictionary construction. (1) Train GloVe word vectors (text2vec in R) on the corpus: 300 dimensions, Xmax = 10, context window 50 tokens, drop the 20 most frequent tokens, tokens in more than 90% of documents, and tokens appearing fewer than 90 times, with AdaGrad (p.6-9). (2) Seeds: 10 uncontroversial positive terms (e.g., "superb", "brilliant", "great") and 10 negative terms (e.g., "bad", "awful", "horrible") (fn.3, p.7). (3) Extract the top 500 positive and top 500 negative words by cosine similarity to the seed-sum vectors, removing SMART stop words and AFINN opposite-valence terms (fn.4, p.7-9). (4) Weight token counts by tf-idf and by cosine similarity to get similarity-weighted positive and negative counts (Wp, Wn). (5) Polarity = (sum Wp - sum Wn) / (sum Wp + sum Wn), centered and scaled for comparison (fn.6, p.8). Accuracy uses a zero cutpoint. Sensitivity tests: corpus size (Figure 2), number of extracted words (appendix), and temporal re-estimation. Validity: benchmark accuracy against assigned ratings (with comparison to LIWC, AFINN, and supervised baselines in Table 1), convergent validity (polarity vs. number of dissenting votes, Figure 3), and discriminant validity (justice-level differences from LIWC and AFINN, Figures 4-5).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper is a measurement-validity paper. Validity is assessed by (a) classification accuracy against the benchmark review ratings, in-sample and on a held-out 25,000-review set; (b) convergent validity with voting divisions (number of dissenting votes); and (c) discriminant validity against LIWC and AFINN justice-level estimates and against historical narratives. The Supreme Court validity evidence is described as "suggestive - though not conclusive" (p.25).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language movie reviews from IMDB (benchmark), and all U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions available from justia.com for 1792-2010 (about 26,000 opinions). Institution: the U.S. Supreme Court. Era: 1792-2010, split into pre-1891 (Evarts Act), 1891-1925 (Judges Act and the start of the consensus norm's decline), and post-1925 windows (p.19-20). Claims are limited to document-level polarity. The paper says the method is not a universal substitute for supervised learning (p.15).

key_findings.finding: Corpus-based dictionary polarity classifies movie reviews more accurately than standard dictionaries. In-sample accuracy is 80.4% (12,004 negative, 12,663 positive, 332 neutral) versus 69.4% for LIWC (with scaling) and 71.3% for AFINN.
key_findings.numbers: 80.4% vs 69.4% (LIWC) vs 71.3% (AFINN); 12,004 neg / 12,663 pos / 332 neutral

key_findings.finding: Out-of-sample (held-out 25,000 reviews) accuracy is consistent with in-sample accuracy: 79.5% for the corpus-based approach, 69.7% for LIWC, and 70.6% for AFINN.
key_findings.numbers: 79.5% (ours, held-out) vs 69.7% (LIWC) vs 70.6% (AFINN)

key_findings.finding: Accuracy gains hold across corpus sizes. Even 5,000-document corpora beat the LIWC and AFINN accuracy figures, and accuracy approaches standard machine-learning levels by about 15,000 documents. Accuracy rises with corpus size, with diminishing returns after about 30,000.

key_findings.finding: Compared with supervised classifiers on the same movie-review benchmark, the approach matches Naive Bayes, MaxEnt, and SVM (about 79-80%) but falls short of Pang and Lee (2004, 87.15%) and Maas et al. (2011, 88.05%). The paper stresses it uses no classification labels.

Only 34.0% of negative and 27.7% of positive terms carry over from the early Court to the turn-of-century Court; only 24.2% of negative and 19.6% of positive terms carry over from the turn-of-century Court to the modern Court.

The corpus-based measure gives Chief Justice White a substantial drop in polarity. Chief Justice Waite is marginally negative in the corpus-based measure, versus marginally positive in LIWC. Historical narratives are cited as support, but the paper calls the evidence suggestive rather than conclusive.

limitations: Not a substitute for supervised learning when labeled benchmarks exist; the paper says it does not argue for universal replacement (p.15).
Measurement is at the document level. It obscures which subjects receive sentiment, and it does not capture sentiment within documents, which matters for long opinions (p.27).
Generalizability to other specialized vocabularies is untested. The paper asks whether the method 'travels well' and flags within-document variation in sentiment-laden word use as a concern (p.27).
Dictionaries may include noisy non-subjective terms; the authors plan to adopt Pang and Lee (2004) subjectivity filtering in future work (p.27).

The Supreme Court validation relies on voting divisions, which the authors call an imperfect proxy because consensual norms mask disagreement, and on historical narratives; the paper calls the result 'suggestive - though not conclusive' (p.17, p.20, p.25).
Temporal splits (pre-1891, 1891-1925, post-1925) are chosen on theoretical grounds; the authors note rolling windows as an alternative for semantic-change studies (fn.14, p.19).
Accuracy is computed with a zero cutpoint, and neutral reviews (332) are excluded from accuracy; LIWC is reported with and without scaling (p.10).
Unlabeled reviews are retained in the word-vector corpus, which the authors describe as a conservative test (p.9, p.14).
Majority opinions only are analyzed; concurrences and dissents are dropped for comparability across eras (p.18).
Terms were not stemmed (fn.13, p.19).
The appendix (corpus-size and seed-set robustness, opinion-length density) is referenced but not in the PDF.

summary_md:
Rice and Zorn (2018, a PSRM revise-and-resubmit draft) argue that off-the-shelf sentiment dictionaries break on specialized vocabularies. Their alternative starts from 10 positive and 10 negative seed words, trains GloVe vectors on the domain corpus (300 dimensions, 50-token window, terms seen fewer than 90 times dropped), keeps the 500 nearest words on each side, weights counts by tf-idf and cosine similarity, and scores polarity as (Wp-Wn)/(Wp+Wn). On 50,000 IMDB reviews this reaches 80.4% in-sample and 79.5% held out, against about 69-71% for LIWC and AFINN. It needs roughly 5,000 or more documents before it beats them. On about 26,000 Supreme Court majority opinions (1792-2010), justice-level polarity ranks correlate only 0.29 with LIWC and 0.16 with AFINN, while those two correlate 0.64 with each other. The choice of dictionary therefore reorders the units. The paper calls its court validation suggestive, not conclusive, and notes that document-level polarity cannot say which subject the sentiment is about.

For Paul's system the sharpest point is Stage 5b. press_value = DEBATE stance sign x stock Lexicoder LSD2015 intensity. LSD lists "credit" as positive and "debt*", "charge*", "risk*", "oversight*" and "fraud*" as negative, and run_stage5.R scores every release with no masking of those domain terms. I ran a quick one-path check on 1,563 text-bearing releases (UNVERIFIED, per DE-062). It found the effect real but small: 4.5% of positive mass and 7.0% of negative mass come from those terms, the release-level intensity rank correlation is 0.953 with and without them, and the LSD net sign flips on 4.1% of releases. The legacy regex scorer cites Rice and Zorn for its polarity formula, but its lexicon is hand-weighted. Its corpus-expansion helper departs from the paper's parameters and was never run. The paper is a measurement template the press layer has not yet applied, not a reason to change rankings.

extraction.title: Using step and path selection functions for estimating resistance to movement: pumas as a case study
extraction.venue: Landscape Ecology (vol. 31, pp. 1319-1335; published online 2 Nov 2015). Special issue: Multi-scale habitat modeling.
extraction.document_type: Journal research article (ecology / landscape connectivity, GPS movement data)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks (text file lines 0-1469): abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusions, acknowledgments and the full reference list. The text file contains no appendices (Appendices 1-7) and no figure images; figures are described only through their captions (Figs 1-7). Paul's markup: the task list was "(none)", so no annotation files were opened and paul_markup is empty. Topic coverage: lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators, allocation, text measurement and political networks are absent from the paper. Network content is limited to landscape connectivity (circuit theory via CircuitScape, current density) and path/step movement models; "path" here means animal movement trajectories, not graph path-finding.
extraction.research_question: Can step selection functions (SSFs) and path selection functions (PathSFs) be extended to model habitat selection during movement at multiple spatial scales, and how sensitive are the regression coefficients and predicted resistance surfaces to (a) SSF vs PathSF, (b) scale, (c) paired vs unpaired prediction framework, and (d) GPS acquisition interval (5 min vs 60 min)?
extraction.theory: Resource selection functions (used vs available design; Johnson 1980 third-order selection; Manly et al. 2002). SSFs (Fortin et al. 2005) and PathSFs (Cushman et al. 2010) are conditional logistic models of movement selection; predicted relative probability exp(sum b_i x_i) is inverted to give resistance. The paper argues that movement-based selection can differ from resource-use (point) selection, citing Squires et al. 2013, Elliot et al. 2014 and Zeller et al. 2014. Scale of analysis is defined as the Pareto-kernel radius (ecological neighborhood), not data grain.
extraction.data: Ten pumas (Puma concolor), six female and four male, Santa Ana Mountains, southern California; Lotek 4400S GPS collars set to 5-min fixes, Oct 2011 to Mar 2014. Collar duration 9-71 days (median 29). Final dataset 75,716 fixes after removing 2D fixes with PDOP above 5 (individual range 1,650-18,464; median 7,147). Unit of analysis: used/available step (steps of 200 m or more, buffered 30 m) and used/available 24-h path (n = 315 paths, 12 start-hour subsets averaged). Land cover: CalVeg vector data at 1:24,000, rasterized to 30 m, aggregated from 25 types to nine classes (chaparral 45%, urban 19%, coastal scrub 14%, annual grassland 6%, coastal oak woodland 5%, agriculture 5%, riparian 3%, perennial grassland 2%, barren/open 1%). Pseudo data: the 5-min data subsampled to 60-min fixes. Study period 2011-2014; no sex-specific analysis (sexes pooled).
extraction.method: Multi-scale SSF and PathSF with Pareto-weighted kernels. 19 time intervals (5 min, 20 min, then every 20 min to 360 min); generalized Pareto fitted per interval with gpd.fit (gPdtest); kernel radius = min(97.5th percentile of displacement, maximum observed displacement), giving scales of 532 to 7,390 m. Available area for each step/path = mean land cover proportion across kernels placed along the step/path. Predictors = differences in land cover proportion between used and available (no intercept, response always 1). Simple single-variable conditional logistic models at each scale; multiple models using the weakest-effect class as reference; characteristic scale = scale with largest absolute coefficient in simple models; multi-scale model combines characteristic scales. Mixed-effects (random puma) conditional logistic models failed to converge, so glm was used. Model performance: 10-fold cross-validation (Johnson et al. 2006) with Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). AIC compared only within SSF and within PathSF (equal sample sizes). Resistance predicted in unpaired (pixel-only) and paired (pixel plus kernel context) frameworks; resistance = 1/probability, not rescaled. Acquisition-interval bias: 60-min pseudo steps and paths treated against 5-min truth; bias = mean absolute difference in coefficients per cover type, averaged per scale. Connectivity: CircuitScape current density between protected areas on either side of I-15 (Temecula corridor); top 20 current-flow pixels along I-15 compared across resistance models.
extraction.scope: Population: ten pumas with established home ranges in one fragmented, urbanizing region (Santa Ana Mountains, southern California). Dispersing animals were not sampled and the authors say results may differ for them. Era: GPS data 2011-2014. Land cover from CalVeg (USDA Forest Service 2007). Methods are presented as general for SSFs/PathSFs at any GPS interval; empirical claims apply only to pumas in this study area.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. Inference rests on the within-animal case-control design (each used step/path is compared with its own available area, which is the standard conditional logistic set-up), plus two internal comparisons: (1) 5-min data as truth versus 60-min subsampled pseudo data for the same animals, to isolate the effect of acquisition interval; (2) paired versus unpaired prediction from the same fitted coefficients, to isolate the effect of prediction framework. Out-of-sample performance is assessed by 10-fold cross-validation with CCC. Cross-method comparisons of AIC are explicitly not made.
measures: Relative probability of movement exp(sum b_i x_i)
Resistance = inverse of predicted relative probability (not rescaled or truncated)
Conditional logistic regression coefficients per land cover class
Land cover proportion difference between used and Pareto-kernel available area
Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (10-fold cross-validated)
AIC (within SSF and within PathSF only)
Bias = mean absolute difference in coefficients (5-min vs 60-min), averaged over cover types per scale
CircuitScape current density (McRae et al. 2008, 2013)
Count of top-20 current-flow pixels along I-15 (road-crossing candidate locations)

key_findings.finding: Regression coefficients are highly sensitive to the scale of analysis. Annual grassland and agriculture change sign across scales. For PathSFs, urban coefficients range about -10 to -30 and chaparral about -4 to -15.
key_findings.numbers: PathSF urban -10 to -30; chaparral -4 to -15; 19 scales from 532 to 7,390 m

key_findings.finding: Pumas show multiple characteristic scales of response during movement, described as mostly bi-modal. Coarse scales characterize urban and agriculture; fine scales characterize the remaining cover types (annual grassland, barren, chaparral, coastal scrub, perennial grassland, and others).
key_findings.numbers: Scales 532 to 7,390 m; 19 time intervals from 5 min to 360 min

key_findings.finding: PathSFs generally produced larger-magnitude coefficients than SSFs. Characteristic scales also differed between the two methods for every cover type except chaparral, most for coastal oak woodland and riparian. Annual grassland was the exception to the larger-PathSF pattern.
key_findings.numbers: Differences in characteristic scale for all types except chaparral

key_findings.finding: Predictive performance (10-fold CCC) rose with scale and PathSFs outperformed SSFs at all scales except the finest (532 m PathSF was the weak case). Best SSF CCC 0.976 at 6,555 m; best PathSF CCC 0.992 at 7,390 m. The multi-scale model did not have the highest CCC but was close: 0.943 (SSF) and 0.982 (PathSF).
key_findings.location: Results, Model performance, Fig. 4 (p. 1326); Discussion p. 1331
key_findings.numbers: SSF best 0.976 (6,555 m); PathSF best 0.992 (7,390 m); multi-scale 0.943 SSF, 0.982 PathSF

key_findings.finding: Within each method, AIC decreased with increasing scale. The multi-scale model had the lowest AIC for SSFs; the 6,555 m model had the lowest AIC for PathSFs. AIC could not be compared between SSFs and PathSFs because sample sizes differed.
key_findings.location: Results, Model performance (pp. 1326-1328, Appendix 3 not in text)
key_findings.numbers: SSF lowest AIC = multi-scale; PathSF lowest AIC = 6,555 m

key_findings.finding: Acquisition interval bias: 60-min pseudo data produced a consistent 3-4-fold difference in regression coefficients relative to 5-min data. Bias was larger for PathSFs than SSFs. Some cover types changed sign. Annual grassland and barren were preferred in 5-min steps but avoided in 60-min pseudo steps. Coastal scrub, avoided in the true steps, appeared preferred in the pseudo steps.
key_findings.location: Results, Acquisition interval bias, Fig. 5 (p. 1328); Discussion (p. 1331)
key_findings.numbers: 3-4-fold consistent difference; 60-min vs 5-min

key_findings.finding: Paired-framework resistance surfaces are more heterogeneous, with a greater range and larger maximum values, than unpaired surfaces. Unpaired surfaces assign one resistance value per cover type regardless of context. In the paired surfaces, urban produces rings of high resistance on entry but low resistance inside.
key_findings.location: Results, Sensitivity of resistance surfaces, Fig. 6, Appendices 5-6 (pp. 1328-1330); Discussion p. 1331-1333
key_findings.numbers: Urban (19% of area) gives highest unpaired resistance; 91st-100th percentile identical across unpaired surfaces

key_findings.finding: Resistance values were higher for PathSFs than SSFs and increased with scale. The finest scale had the lowest resistance range, especially for SSFs. The authors attribute the scale trend to coefficients becoming more negative as scale increases.
key_findings.numbers: Finest scale lowest range; resistance increases with scale

key_findings.finding: Road-crossing candidate locations (top 20 current-flow pixels along I-15) differed between SSF and PathSF, among scales, and between prediction frameworks. Locations were more similar at the same scale across methods and frameworks than within the same method across scales, so scale is a major driver of connectivity differences. Pseudo-step (60-min) models biased crossing locations and missed middle-I-15 sites, and SSF models also flagged sites absent from true-path models.
key_findings.location: Results p. 1330 (Fig. 7, Appendix 7 not in text); Discussion p. 1331
key_findings.numbers: Top 20 pixels along I-15 per model

key_findings.finding: Authors recommend PathSF models over SSFs when a choice is available, and caution that resistance surfaces and corridors are sensitive to method, scale and GPS schedule.

limitations: Only ten pumas, with sexes pooled; mixed-effects models with individual as random effect failed to converge, so glm was used and individual heterogeneity was not modeled (p. 1325).
Only land cover predictors were used; slope, topographic ruggedness and roads, known to affect puma selection, were excluded to simplify the methods (p. 1332).
Study animals had established home ranges; the authors state results may not hold for dispersers, who may select habitat at finer scales (p. 1331-1332).
The inverse of predicted relative probability is assumed to equal resistance; the authors state no empirical evidence supports this (p. 1333).

Whether the paired framework is superior to the unpaired framework, or a hybrid, is unresolved; the paired surfaces may not capture absolute fitness costs, and the authors note concerns about rings of high resistance around urban areas (pp. 1328-1333).
Resistance surfaces were compared visually and by distributional summaries only; no method for whole-surface validation was provided beyond road-crossing locations (p. 1333).
Connectivity analysis is a single illustrative CircuitScape run in one corridor (Temecula / I-15) and was described as cursory (p. 1326).
Bias was assessed only at one alternative interval (60 min); the optimal acquisition interval for pumas was not determined, and a shorter-than-5-min interval may be better (p. 1332).
AIC cannot be compared between SSFs and PathSFs because sample sizes differ, limiting method-level model selection.
The scale of analysis is the Pareto-kernel radius, and the grain was held at 30 m; the effect of grain was not examined.
The 24-h path analysis averages over 12 start-time subsets rather than estimating a single model.
Brownian bridge alternatives were suggested but not tested (p. 1333).

short_quotes.quote: Regression coefficients were extremely sensitive to scale and pumas exhibited multiple scales of selection during movement.
Given our results, when there is a choice, we recommend PathSF models be used over SSF models.
a mismatch between GPS collar acquisition interval and species vagility may ultimately bias corridor conservation planning

summary_md:
Zeller et al. (2016) used GPS tracks from ten pumas in the Santa Ana Mountains (75,716 fixes at 5-minute intervals, 2011-2014) to fit two kinds of conditional-logistic movement model. Step selection functions (SSFs) compare each observed step with available alternatives. Path selection functions (PathSFs) do the same for whole 24-hour paths. Both were fitted at 19 Pareto-kernel scales from 532 m to 7,390 m. The predicted relative probability was inverted to give a resistance surface, which CircuitScape then used to locate road-crossing candidates on I-15.

Main results:
- **Scale.** Coefficients are very sensitive to scale. Some cover types change sign, and PathSF urban coefficients run from about -10 to -30.
- **Method.** PathSFs fit better under 10-fold cross-validation (CCC 0.992 vs 0.976 for SSFs).
- **Sampling interval.** Coarsening fixes to 60 minutes shifts coefficients 3-4 fold and flips some signs.
- **Crossing locations.** These change with method, scale and prediction framework, and scale is the biggest driver.
- **Unvalidated core step.** The authors say no empirical evidence supports treating resistance as the inverse of probability.

The paper has nothing on lobbying, legislators or political networks. It matters here only by analogy, and only in one place: the path-finding layer turns modelled tie strength or probability into an additive cost (-log p or -ln(0.8·strength)) and then takes the cheapest route. The paper is a close case study showing that this kind of probability-to-cost inversion is an assumption, and that the routes it produces depend on scale and sampling choices. It also gives a template for testing such costs: compare the routes actually used against available alternatives in a case-control design. The staffer-route search already labels its cost as "not a probability of access", which fits both the paper's caution and D-025. What it lacks is any used-vs-available calibration, which PathSF would supply if an outreach log ever exists. All transfer is analogical (animals on land cover, not people in organisations). Strength is weak throughout. This analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Resistance is set to the inverse of the predicted relative probability, exp(sum b_i x_i), and the authors state that no empirical evidence supports equating that inverse with resistance. The routes and crossing locations it produces (top-20 current-flow pixels on I-15) shift with method (SSF vs PathSF), with scale (532-7,390 m) and with the paired vs unpaired framework.
bearings.paper_location: Methods (resistance = 1/probability, not rescaled); Discussion p. 1333; Results p. 1330, Fig. 7
bearings.system_side: Route cost is a parallel inversion. Each hop costs -ln(0.8 x strength) plus a weighted uncertainty term, and bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 returns the minimum-cost route. The code already labels the score 'not a probability of access' and calls u 'not a probability'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Analogy only. In the paper, a fitted selection probability on a 30 m landscape becomes a cost. Here, hand-set exposure strengths between people become a cost. What carries over is the methodological warning: the probability-to-cost transform is an untested assumption, and route choice is sensitive to it. That supports the system's existing non-probability wording (D-025). It gives no evidence about which transform is right for staffer ties.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Staffer closeness route search|Staffer closeness route search]]

bearings.paper_claim: PathSF compares each observed path with its own set of available alternatives in a conditional-logistic case-control design, and so estimates cost coefficients from observed route choices. It outperformed step-wise SSF at every scale except the finest (10-fold CCC 0.992 vs 0.976), and the authors recommend PathSF when there is a choice.
bearings.paper_location: Methods (PathSF, used/available paths, n = 315); Results Fig. 4 p. 1326; Conclusions p. 1334
bearings.system_side: The component's open question is whether shorter or cheaper routes match successful real introductions in an outreach log. Its costs (HOP_FACTOR 0.8, uncertainty weight, 5-year staleness half-life) are assumptions, not fitted values. The module states its costs are 'not fitted success or friendship probabilities'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This only applies if an outreach log of attempted and completed introductions is ever recorded. Each used route could then be paired with Yen-alternative routes as the available set, and conditional-logistic weights could be fitted for the hop-cost components. Until then it is a design template, not evidence. Any fitted output would stay a heuristic score, never an access or introduction probability (D-025), and would need a single-look holdout.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Staffer closeness route search|Staffer closeness route search]]

bearings.paper_claim: Whole-path selection (PathSF) gives coefficients of larger magnitude than step-wise selection (SSF), and different characteristic scales for every cover type except chaparral. The road-crossing sites also differ between step-based and path-based models. Composing steps does not reproduce whole-path behaviour.
bearings.paper_location: Results p. 1326 and p. 1330; Discussion p. 1331
bearings.system_side: The recruitment chain is ranked by the product of independent per-hop cosponsor-kernel probabilities (Dijkstra on -log p, then pathReliability). chainHold multiplies the per-hop activeP values, with ASKM 0.07 treated as constant and unestimated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Loose analogy. The paper shows that animal movement along a whole path is not the composition of independent steps. Legislators recruited through a chain may likewise not act as independent hops. The evidence concerns habitat selection, not social asks, so it only motivates checking hop independence against observed cosponsor join sequences. It does not show that the product rule is wrong here.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Sponsor-to-target max-product path and chain hold|Sponsor-to-target max-product path and chain hold]]

gaps_exposed: No used-vs-available (case-control) calibration of any route cost: the staffer and recruitment path costs are hand-set transforms of strength or probability and have never been fitted to observed route choices or successful introductions.

No sensitivity report showing how the returned top route changes when the cost transform (-ln vs 1/p vs linear) or the tie-strength time window changes. The paper shows that the cost-surface and route choices can be the dominant source of route differences.
No test of whether multi-hop recruitment behaves like independent hops (step-wise) or like a whole path. Chain reliability assumes independence.
flags: Wording guard (D-025): the paper's 'resistance' and 'relative probability of movement' language must not be imported to describe staffer or recruitment routes as closeness, access or introduction probabilities. The current code wording ('not a probability of access') already complies.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Nothing to flag there.
All bearings are analogical, cross-domain (puma movement on land cover) and UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul's pathfinding notes call for learned heuristics, A*-style handling of unstable information, and dynamic replanning. The built staffer router uses heuristic 0 and hand-set costs. This paper does not speak to heuristics. It adds a caution Paul's notes lack: the step that turns a probability into a cost is itself an unvalidated assumption, and route outputs are sensitive to it. It also offers a way to learn costs from observed paths (PathSF), which fits his wish for learned components. His annotations are not stale here; they simply do not cover cost calibration. Paul left no markup on this paper.

related.why: The recruitment chain runs a most-reliable-path search (Dijkstra on -log p). Zeller shows that the probability-to-cost inversion behind such searches is an assumption whose route outputs depend on how the probabilities were estimated.
Both turn tie strength into path cost for shortest-path search. Zeller adds a way to fit that transform empirically (used vs available paths) rather than setting it by hand.
Lawande covers grid and waypoint path-finding algorithms on a given cost surface. Zeller covers how such a cost surface is estimated and how sensitive the resulting routes are to it.

backlinks.why: Both papers infer movement cost or access from observed movement rather than straight-line distance: Zeller estimates resistance to movement with step and path selection functions, and Esmalian uses trip time vs trip distance. Both are relevant to any travel-cost weighting in the Terrier turf planner.

extraction.title: Machine and deep learning for personality traits detection: a comprehensive survey and open research challenges
extraction.venue: Artificial Intelligence Review 58:239 (accepted 25 April 2025; published online 9 May 2025). Metadata hint verified against the PDF text; no correction needed.
extraction.document_type: Systematic literature review and survey (narrative plus tabulated comparison), with one comparative empirical experiment on the MBTI Kaggle dataset. Not a meta-analysis; no pooled effect sizes.
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (3,686 lines, front matter through references and author block) in chunks. Figures 1-11 appear only as captions in the text layer, so their plotted content was not reviewed. Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied ("none"), so paul_markup is empty. Page numbers below are manuscript page numbers from the "Page N of 57" running markers.
extraction.research_question: Six research questions (Sec 3, p.3; answered in Sec 13, pp.45-46): RQ1 Which ML models suit personality trait detection in online text? RQ2 Which DL models suit it? RQ3 How do diverse features and ML/DL models affect accuracy? RQ4 What features and dataset sources exist? RQ5 What application areas exist and how do they affect fields? RQ6 What open research challenges exist and what strategies address them?
extraction.theory: No single theory is tested. Background personality frameworks are summarized (Sec 6, pp.8-10, Table 4): MBTI (four dichotomies, 16 types), Big Five/OCEAN, HEXACO (adds Honesty-Humility), PEN (adds Psychoticism), and DISC (Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, Conscientiousness). The authors state they integrate psychological theory with computational linguistics (Sec 4, p.4) but do not show an operational model linking text features to constructs.
extraction.data: Literature corpus: 305 initial search hits (IEEE Xplore, Springer, DBLP, ACM, MDPI, Google Scholar) narrowed to 171 primary studies (Sec 5, p.7). The text says the search covers "the last five-year literature" (p.6), while the cited works span 2018-2025. Empirical experiment (Sec 9, pp.25-32): the Kaggle MBTI dataset, unit = text sample or post labeled with one of 16 MBTI types. Sample size is not stated in Sec 9.1 (p.25). Sec 10.2 (p.34) states 8,675 volunteers, "fifty tweet texts" each, and 422,845 labeled data points; these figures are internally inconsistent (8,675 x 50 = 433,750), and Table 13 (p.33) lists 8,600 instances. Dataset survey: 14 textual personality datasets (Table 13, pp.33-37). Results tables (10-12) report Big Five trait labels (Extroversion, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness, Openness) on what is described as the MBTI dataset; the mapping is not explained.
extraction.method: Systematic-style review: keyword search strings (p.6, Table 3 p.10), duplicate and title screening, abstract screening, full review, and quality questions on domain and venue (p.7; criteria not reported in detail). Taxonomy by shallow ML, ensemble, sequential DL (RNN/CNN/LSTM/Bi-LSTM/GRU), and transformers (Sec 7, pp.11-20; Tables 5-8). Preprocessing: lowercasing, URL/punctuation/number removal, stop-word removal, lemmatization and stemming, tokenization (Sec 7.1, pp.11-13; Sec 9.1, p.25). Features: TF-IDF, POS tags, BoW, N-grams, Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText, sentence embeddings (Sec 7.2, pp.13-14; Sec 9.2, p.26). Models: SVM, NB, LR, DT, KNN, GB, RF, XGBoost, AdaBoost, LSTM, Bi-LSTM, BERT, DistilBERT (Sec 9.3, pp.26-27). Empirical comparison is tabulated accuracy only (Tables 10-12).
extraction.identification: None. Descriptive and comparative review; no causal design, no instrument validation, no inferential statistics.
extraction.scope: Population: English-language social media and related user-generated text (Twitter, Facebook, Reddit, forums, YouTube transcripts, essays, dialogue corpora). Era: studies roughly 2018-2025. Institutions: none; the authors are from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. The text says the focus is natural language content, not image, video, or audio (Sec 14, p.47). Lobbying, legislators, path-finding, allocation, turnout, and persuasion are absent. Elections appear only in passing (intro citation of Zarouali et al. 2024, p.2; political campaign paragraph, p.39).

summary_md:
Naz et al. (2025) is a survey of machine-learning and deep-learning methods that detect personality from text. It covers 171 studies, selected from 305 search hits by a screening funnel whose numbers do not add up. It sorts methods into shallow ML, ensembles, sequential deep learning and transformers, catalogues 14 text datasets (several of them no longer available), and runs one experiment on the Kaggle MBTI data. In that experiment, Bi-LSTM with sentence embeddings (Extraversion 92, Agreeableness 91) and DistilBERT (Openness 92, Conscientiousness 91) beat TF-IDF SVM (Openness 89, Conscientiousness 80).

The empirical part is weak. It reports accuracy only, with no train/test split, cross-validation, class balance or variance. It reports Big Five traits on a dataset labeled with MBTI types and never explains the mapping. Its text and tables disagree in several places. Its Table 9 ranks results from different papers as if they used the same data and protocol. The authors' answer to their research questions is that transformers and deep embeddings perform best, while traditional ML stays interpretable and competitive on small data.

For Paul's system the paper is mostly context. Its population is ordinary social-media users who labeled their own personality type. The system instead measures legislators' public speech and checks it against expert and insider panels and against the Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh (RKH) congressional estimates, using single-look held-out correlations. The paper's accuracy figures are not comparable to the system's held-out r (mean .350 vs RKH) and should not be quoted as benchmarks. Two points do carry over. First, the paper states that personality datasets do not directly measure emotional stability or neuroticism, which matches the system's record that no gold criterion exists for N. Second, its finding that classical TF-IDF models stay competitive on small labeled sets matches the stance stack's measured result: LinearSVC at 83.9% beat the transformer at 0.757 on 87 test rows. That second point tempers Paul's view that bag-of-words SVMs are outdated.

bearings.paper_claim: Deep and transformer readers beat TF-IDF/closed-vocabulary shallow ML at trait detection. MBTI experiment: Bi-LSTM + sentence embeddings Ext 92 / Cons 90 / Agr 91 / Open 89; DistilBERT Open 92 / Cons 91; SVM (TF-IDF) Open 89 / Cons 80; POS-DT Cons about 53. The paper reports accuracy only, with no split, cross-validation or variance.
bearings.system_side: The lexical reader works in the style of Ramey et al. It z-scores LIWC-analog, Empath, MATTR and concreteness rates within this corpus and combines them with published-correlate or SMOreg weights, which are then refit to RKH with ridge or LinearSVR. Held-out CV r vs RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214 (mean .350). Members with fewer than 1,500 tokens are flagged lowconf, and consumers shrink them toward 0.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak transfer. The paper's labels are MBTI types that ordinary social-media users reported about themselves, its unit is the post or user, and its metric is accuracy on dichotomized traits. The system's targets are expert and insider ratings or RKH estimates for about 147 to 533 legislators, scored by held-out correlation. Fine-tuning a deep reader would need thousands of labeled members, and the system has no such set. The paper therefore gives no usable effect size for replacing the lexical reader, and its accuracies must not be compared with the system's r.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)|Lexical Big Five (Ramey-style closed vocabulary)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Text personality datasets lack a direct measure of emotional stability or neuroticism (Sec 1, p.2). The survey's experiment reports only Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness and Openness, with no N/ES result.
bearings.system_side: affective_n combines a Pennebaker LIWC base (first-person singular, negative and positive emotion) with LLM affective facets, controlled for party. Because no gold N criterion exists, its gate tests construct integrity only. Genre transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050, .161).
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a statement about the field, not a test. It confirms that the literature offers no ready-made N criterion the system has missed. It does not validate the system's affective-N construct. It applies regardless of population, because the gap concerns the datasets themselves.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests|Affective neuroticism slot and N genre-transfer tests]]

bearings.paper_claim: Traditional ML (SVM and similar on TF-IDF) remains interpretable and competitive on small data. Deep and transformer gains appear with large labeled corpora. The text claims about a 25% LSTM gain over traditional ML, but no table supports the figure.
bearings.system_side: The best classical stance reader is LinearSVC on word (1-2 gram) plus char_wb (3-5 gram) TF-IDF: 83.9% accuracy and macro-F1 .816 on 87 untouched test rows, versus a transformer at 0.757 on the same comparison. Supervised tweet stance reached 0.737 CV on 399 golds.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper studies personality, not stance, so this is a pattern about small labeled sets of a few hundred rows, not stance evidence. It fits the system's measured outcome. It does not show that transformers lose at larger n, and it says nothing about LLM zero-shot readers (Birkenmaier, Kim J.), which Paul's view rests on.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Supervised and stacked stance readers|Supervised and stacked stance readers]]

bearings.paper_claim: LLMs are listed as an open challenge and future direction for personality detection, without an evaluation. BERT and GPT are named most effective in the RQ answers. The paper does not discuss identity leakage, reputational priors or halo.
bearings.system_side: The item-level LLM reader removes author identity (name, state, party, title) before scoring, codes 'cannot tell' as 0, and averages 1,200-word chunks. It is display-only, and its behavioural diagonal mean of +0.064 falls short of the 0.12 bar. The ridge hybrid combines lexical, interaction and persona features under nested CV against behavioural targets.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The system's LLM design is already more careful than anything the survey covers (de-identification, observer-keyed items, held-out behavioural criteria). The paper adds no evidence that would move the reader off display-only status.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model|LLM item-level reader (Pink), ridge hybrid and CT-CM latent model]]

gaps_exposed: The system has no labeled corpus large enough to fine-tune a transformer trait reader on legislators. Every reader is either closed-vocabulary with weights fit to RKH, or a zero-shot LLM. The survey's best results all depend on thousands of labeled users.

The survey treats sentence embeddings with a Bi-LSTM or DistilBERT as the strongest representation. The system's lexical reader has no embedding-based variant tested under the single-look protocol against RKH or the gold panels. This is a possible candidate, but it would need its own preregistration and remains UNVERIFIED.
The survey names XAI and multimodal fusion (text plus audio) as open challenges. The system's audio prosody channel already MISSed (N=90) and is display-only, so the survey offers no new route there.
flags: Do not quote this paper's accuracies (88-92%) as benchmarks for the system's trait readers. They are accuracy-only, with no train/test split, cross-validation or variance reported. They are Big Five labels on an MBTI-typed dataset with no stated mapping, and text and tables disagree (Sec 9.5 GloVe 85 vs Table 11 89; Sec 7.5 79-85% vs Table 9 90).

Table 9 ranks accuracies compiled from different studies with different protocols and calls them results on 'the same dataset'. That is not a like-for-like comparison, so no ranking from it should enter brain notes.
The screening funnel does not reconcile (305 -> 270, 184 excluded, 171 final), and the MBTI sample counts conflict (8,675 x 50 vs 422,845 vs 8,600). Treat the review's coverage claims as approximate.

The survey mentions applications to political microtargeting and social influence (Sec 11, pp.39-40), but it provides no evidence that detected traits predict response to persuasion. Nothing here validates the receptivity layer's trait-to-susceptibility weights, whose sign choices remain design priors.
There is no conflict with D-025, D-021, the rejected SNA proposals, or the reciprocity rulings. The paper does not touch networks or lobbying.
paul_alignment: There is no annotation from Paul on this paper. It partly agrees and partly disagrees with his reading elsewhere. It agrees with his endorsement of transformer and LLM readers (via Birkenmaier and Kim J.) in that it ranks BERT and GPT highest. It also tempers his highlighted view that bag-of-words SVM baselines are outdated: the survey's own conclusion is that classical models stay competitive on small labeled sets, and the system's stance stack measured exactly that (LinearSVC 83.9% vs transformer 0.757, n=87). On personality, Paul calls Ramey 'dated but foundational'. This survey neither replaces Ramey for legislators nor supplies a validated alternative, because none of its data are politicians and none of its measures use expert ratings. The system's record (lexical traits indicted for behavioural prediction, the LLM reader display-only, N without a gold criterion) remains more pessimistic, and better evidenced, than this survey's optimism. His notes on LLM trait reading should be read alongside that record.

related.why: Cited as the deep-learning artifact for text-based personality measurement, which is the strongest measurement-validity work in the survey's reference list.
A meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes for Big Five prediction from social-media footprints. It supplies the quantitative synthesis this narrative survey lacks.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five relations, which bounds what the closed-vocabulary features the survey treats as baseline (and the system's lexical reader) can recover.
The system's lexical reader copies Ramey's pipeline for legislators. The survey covers the general-population ML lineage, which does not address elites.
A validated politician-specific LLM trait reading (agency and communion, Krippendorff alpha, macro-F1). It is the counterpart for political elites that this survey does not cover.
Another review of personality computing that covers the same ML pipeline families and their threats.
Predicts the Big Five from Twitter text, the shallow-ML setting the survey catalogues.
Compares fine-tuned RoBERTa with traditional ML on political-tweet stance, the same classical-versus-transformer comparison applied to the stance task the system actually runs.

meta.title: Automatic construction of direction-aware sentiment lexicon using direction-dependent words
meta.venue: Language Resources and Evaluation, vol. 59, pp. 843-869 (accepted 28 Mar 2024; published online 25 May 2024)

extraction.title: Automatic construction of direction-aware sentiment lexicon using direction-dependent words
extraction.venue: Language Resources and Evaluation, vol. 59, pp. 843-869 (accepted 28 Mar 2024; published online 25 May 2024)
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (all ~1,684 lines: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-6, Appendix 1, data/funding statements, references, author affiliations). Tables 1-9 were read from the extracted text, which garbles some table layouts; the numbers quoted below are as they appear in that text and should be checked against the PDF table before reuse. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this item, so paul_markup is empty. The _annots folder was not opened for this paper. Scope relevance: text measurement (lexicon construction, PMI co-occurrence, sentence classification) only. Nothing in the paper concerns lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, or legislators.
extraction.research_question: Can a financial sentiment lexicon be built automatically so that each entry is a pair of a directional word (up/down) and a direction-dependent word, so that sentiment flips correctly with direction (e.g., "cost" negative, but "cost decrease" positive)? Does adding these pairs to the Loughran-McDonald (LM) word list improve sentence-level sentiment classification of financial headlines? (Sect. 1, pp. 845-846)
extraction.theory: Lexicon-based explainability: sentiment lexicons are preferred in finance because they expose the words that drive a decision, whereas supervised deep models are black boxes (Sect. 1, pp. 845-846). Domain-specific polarity: a word's sentiment depends on domain and on directional modifiers. Direction-dependency is operationalized as a word whose sentiment orientation changes with "up" or "down" words (Sect. 1, p. 846; Sect. 3.1, p. 850). No formal economic theory is stated beyond the market-sentiment and media literature cited in the introduction (Tetlock 2007; Engelberg and Parsons 2011; Garcia 2013).
extraction.data: Unit: sentence or economic news headline. Construction corpus: DS50 subset of the Financial PhraseBank (FPB), 4,835 English sentences labelled by 16 finance experts; 691 sentences tagged "proportional" and 28 tagged "inversely proportional" after the direction-score step; 56 direction-dependent words extracted; Senti-DD lexicon of 1,767 pairs (1,077 positive, 690 negative) (Sect. 4.1, p. 853; Table 1, p. 848). Evaluation corpora: FPB subsets DS50 (4,835), DS66 (4,209), DS75 (3,447), DS100 (2,259); SemEval-2017 Task 5 subtask 2 (960 messages, continuous scores converted to three classes); FiQA Task 1 (436 sentences) (Sect. 4.3, pp. 855-856; Table 6, p. 856). Directional word lists: 20 "up" and 11 "down" terms seeded from HGI word lists (Table 3, p. 853). Time period: not stated for the corpora; the appendix examples are dated roughly 2006-2010. Evaluation uses stratified five-fold cross-validation repeated five times (Sect. 4.3, p. 856).
extraction.method: Stage 1 (direction tagging, Sect. 3.1): each polar sentence gets a direction score = count of "up" words minus count of "down" words (Porter stemming, NLTK). Sentences are tagged "proportional" (positive with score > 0, or negative with score < 0) or "inversely proportional" (the reverse). Neutral sentences are excluded. Stage 2 (association, Sect. 3.2): nouns are lemmatized (NLTK); nouns occurring in fewer than 1% of sentences are dropped. PMI(w,t) = log2 [p(w,t) / (p(w) p(t))] is computed for each noun and tag. Dependency score (Eq. 1) keeps PMI(w,tp) if PMI(w,tp) - PMI(w,ti) > delta, uses -PMI(w,ti) if the difference is below -delta, and 0 otherwise; delta = 0 in this study. Stage 3 (extraction, Sect. 3.3): from each sentence, the highest-scoring proportional word or the lowest-scoring inversely proportional word is kept as the direction-dependent word; words with non-alphabetic characters or fewer than k = 3 letters are removed. Stage 4 (Senti-DD, Sect. 3.4): pairs of directional and direction-dependent words are labelled positive-context or negative-context. Stage 5 (evaluation, Sect. 4.2): LM sentiment score = PosScore - NegScore (Eq. 2); ContextScore = ContPosScore - ContNegScore (Eq. 3); RefinedScore = SentimentScore + ContextScore (Eq. 4); sign of the refined score gives positive, neutral or negative. Baselines: Sentiment140, SentiWordNet, SO-CAL, MPQA, TextBlob, VADER, SentiStrength, AFINN, LM. Pretrained comparators: Word2Vec with logistic regression (word2vec-google-news-300), BERT-base-uncased and RoBERTa-base fine-tuned (Adam, weight decay 0.01, batch 8, 500 warm-up steps, 3 epochs; Sect. 4.4, pp. 856-857). Hyperparameters were set heuristically, and the authors state that tuning is left to future work (p. 857).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper does not identify any causal effect. Validity rests on the downstream classification F1 of the augmented lexicon against baselines, with the explainability of individual pairs checked by inspection (Appendix 1, pp. 863-866; Table 9, p. 861). The paper says that evaluating lexicon quality directly needs inter-annotator agreement that it did not collect (Sect. 4.2, p. 854).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language economic and financial news headlines (FPB, SemEval-2017 Task 5, FiQA), mainly company-performance headlines from Finnish and other European firms that reflect the FPB corpus. Institution: Seoul National University (Industrial Engineering). Era: the corpora are dated to the mid-2000s to 2010s; the paper does not state a period for its sample. The method is claimed for other domains such as electronics reviews, and for central-bank communications (FOMC) as future work (Sect. 6, pp. 862-863). These extensions were not tested.

key_findings.finding: Senti-DD construction yields 56 direction-dependent words (49 proportional, 7 inversely proportional), e.g., proportional: profit, revenue, growth, net; inversely proportional: cost, plant, traffic.
key_findings.numbers: 56 words; 49 proportional, 7 inversely proportional

key_findings.finding: The lexicon has 1,767 directional/direction-dependent pairs, 1,077 positive and 690 negative.
key_findings.numbers: 1,767 pairs; 1,077 positive; 690 negative

key_findings.finding: Worked PMI example for profit: PMI(profit, proportional) = 0.05 and PMI(profit, inversely proportional) = -3.0, giving dependency score 0.05.
key_findings.numbers: PMI 0.05 and -3.0; dependency score 0.05; 217 sentences contain profit

key_findings.finding: On the four FPB subsets, LM + Senti-DD raises weighted F1 over the LM list alone. The reported F1 values are DS50 0.5914 to 0.7057, DS66 0.6023 to 0.7322, DS75 0.6174 to 0.7788 and DS100 0.5982 to 0.8233. The paper says it beats all lexicon baselines.
On DS100, LM+Senti-DD roughly doubles the negative-class F1 of LM (text says nearly twice). Table values: negative F1 0.4087 (LM) to 0.7260; positive F1 0.2596 (LM) to 0.7361.

On the SemEval and FiQA sets, LM+Senti-DD is still below 0.5 F1 (0.4789 SemEval; 0.4937 FiQA). Pretrained models do better on nearly all measures, and the authors attribute this to lexicon methods needing explicit sentiment words.
key_findings.numbers: F1 SemEval LM 0.3632 -> LM+Senti-DD 0.4789; FiQA LM 0.3635 -> LM+Senti-DD 0.4937

key_findings.finding: The DS100 pretrained models score higher than LM+Senti-DD (e.g., RoBERTa F1 0.9620 on DS100 in the Table 7 text), so the lexicon does not reach state-of-the-art accuracy. The paper says this is an explainability trade-off.
key_findings.location: Table 7 p. 859; Sect. 5 p. 858; Sect. 6 p. 862
key_findings.numbers: RoBERTa DS100 weighted F1 0.9620 as extracted

key_findings.finding: Worked example: LM labels 'Profit for the period was EUR 10.9 mn, down from EUR 14.3 mn in 2009' neutral, but LM+Senti-DD labels it negative via the (profit, down) pair (refined score -1).
key_findings.location: Sect. 5 p. 857; Table 5 p. 855; Fig. 3 p. 858
key_findings.numbers: SentimentScore 0; ContextScore -1; RefinedScore -1

key_findings.finding: In a 20-sentence DS100 sample, 10 predictions are correct and 10 are wrong. Failures mainly come from context pairs the lexicon counts as non-neutral, e.g., (company, increase).
key_findings.numbers: 10 of 20 correct

key_findings.finding: Only 28 of 719 sentences in the construction corpus are inversely proportional, and this imbalance produces noisy direction-dependent words such as beer and day.
key_findings.numbers: 28 inversely proportional sentences; 691 proportional

limitations: Directional word lists are chosen manually by the researchers, which the authors call time-consuming and subjective; the directional vocabulary may also go out of date (Sect. 6, p. 863).
Imbalance between proportional (691) and inversely proportional (28) tagged sentences yields noisy words such as beer and day (Sect. 5, p. 862).
Neutrality is detected passively (equal positive and negative counts), not by a dedicated neutrality step (Sect. 6, p. 863).
Lexicon methods degrade when sentiment is not explicitly expressed; SemEval and FiQA F1 stay below 0.5 (Sect. 5, p. 858).
Pretrained model inference is treated as black box; the paper's statements about why pretrained models succeed are speculative (Sect. 5, p. 858).
Hyperparameters, including the number of epochs and delta = 0, k = 3, were set heuristically; no hyperparameter tuning was done (Sect. 4.4, p. 857).
Evaluation relies on downstream classification F1 without inter-annotator agreement measures; the authors say lexicon quality is hard to assess directly (Sect. 4.2, p. 854).
Sentence-level only, English-only, and mostly headline-length texts; generalization to other domains (electronics reviews, FOMC minutes) is proposed but untested (Sect. 6, pp. 862-863).
Table 7 and Table 8 values in the extracted text are layout-garbled; the reported results have no significance tests or confidence intervals in the text read.
Appendix examples show the lexicon can flag a context pair (company, increase) as a negative cue, which reduces accuracy on some headlines (Sect. 5, p. 862).

summary_md:
Park, Lee and Cho build a financial sentiment lexicon in which each entry pairs a directional word ("up" or "down" family) with a noun whose polarity depends on that direction. Their example is "cost", which is negative alone but positive in "cost decrease". Sentences in the Financial PhraseBank are tagged proportional or inversely proportional from an up-count minus down-count score. PMI between nouns and the two tags picks out 56 direction-dependent words, and these yield 1,767 pairs. Adding the pairs to Loughran-McDonald raises weighted F1 on the PhraseBank subsets from about 0.59-0.62 to 0.71-0.82. On SemEval and FiQA it stays below 0.5, and fine-tuned RoBERTa is far ahead (about 0.96 on DS100). The construction set was heavily imbalanced (28 inversely proportional sentences against 691 proportional), which produced noisy words. Evaluation covers headline-length sentences only, with no significance tests.

This paper has already been used in Paul's system. The brain notes say he adapted it as a "directional verb x CU-valenced target" override for the CFPB sign-flip problem. A whole-text version made 46 sign changes on gold: 3 good and 43 bad. It was rejected because releases defending the CFPB describe the attack with "shrink" verbs. The idea that survives in the built system is a curated, direction-separated target registry (cfpb_reform +1, cfpb_expansion -1, cfpb_institution 0), not an automatic lexicon. The paper explains both results. Its pairs work on short headlines where the direction word modifies the noun, and press releases are long, multi-actor texts. The paper's own failure cases (pairs like company/increase) and its class imbalance match the churn seen in Paul's dry run. The open question in the system (restrict the rule to the sentence or headline that names the bill) is the condition under which the paper's evidence would actually transfer. Nothing here concerns networks, money or allocation.

bearings.paper_claim: On four FPB subsets (DS50 4,835 / DS66 4,209 / DS75 3,447 / DS100 2,259 sentences) LM+Senti-DD weighted F1 is 0.7057, 0.7322, 0.7788, 0.8233 vs LM alone 0.5914, 0.6023, 0.6174, 0.5982. On SemEval-2017 (960 messages) and FiQA (436 sentences) it is 0.4789 and 0.4937, below several general lexicons. In the 20-case DS100 appendix sample 10 are correct and 10 wrong; cited failures include (profit, increase) and (company, increase).
bearings.paper_location: Table 7 pp. 858-859; Sect. 4.3 pp. 855-856 (datasets); Sect. 5 pp. 857-858; Sect. 5 p. 862 and Appendix 1 pp. 863-866
bearings.system_side: Sign comes from DEBATE or the human overlay for text-bearing releases; the bill table supplies sign only for text-less billstatus rows (run_stage5.R lines 128-143). The directional-verb override derived from this paper was tested on whole release text and rejected (3 good / 43 bad sign changes on gold, per brain note). run_stage5.R lines 105-108 document a different rejected experiment (bill-sign override, accuracy 0.839 to 0.770, 2026-06-30) that the rel did not cite.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Evidence transfers only where a directional word governs the target noun inside one short sentence, as in FPB headlines. It does not transfer to whole-release counting over multi-actor congressional press text, where speaker attitude toward the direction is a second hop the paper does not model. The paper's own shift to SemEval and FiQA drops lexicon F1 below 0.5. This supports restricting any rule to the sentence naming the bill; any such variant stays UNVERIFIED until a held-out gold look (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Table 7 and 8 numbers check out once the 13 columns are counted; the layout is not garbled. Rel's 'headline-length, single-actor' is wrong: scope is one-sentence headlines (Sect. 3.1) and 'single-actor' appears nowhere. 'Beats all lexicon baselines' holds on FPB only; on SemEval and FiQA, Sentiment140 (0.5175 SemEval), VADER (0.5447, 0.5513) and AFINN (0.5331, 0.5403) beat LM+Senti-DD. Major omission: the lexicon was built from labels on all 4,835 DS50 sentences (Table 9, Sect. 4.1) and scored on DS50 and DS100 with no described fold-wise rebuild, so the FPB gains are not held-out.

bearings.paper_claim: Polarity attaches to a (direction, target) pair. Direction-dependent nouns are typed proportional or inversely proportional by PMI against direction-tagged sentences (Eq. 1, delta = 0). Of 719 tagged sentences, 691 are proportional and 28 inversely proportional, and the imbalance yields noisy words such as beer and day.

bearings.system_side: Valence is attached per target family in derive_valence_registry.py. cfpb_institution and cfpb_general are fixed at 0 by user-directed policy and act as binding overrides. cfpb_reform and cfpb_expansion have no hard-coded sign; they take whatever sign the gold labels derive. The code keeps families at 75 percent gold consistency (min_consist=0.75) although the file header says 80 percent. Brain note: CFPB is 64% inverse under sentence-level typing and 41% under release-level typing (share of inverse tags, not accuracy). The gold-derived registry scores 0.782 accuracy in honest 5-fold CV against a flat 0.677 baseline; five auto-registry variants scored 0.464 to 0.604.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul's registry is a gold-derived analogue of the paper's direction-pair lexicon; the automatic PMI typing is the part that did not transfer. Transfer is limited by scale: 400 tweet golds and 238 distinct targets, against the paper's 4,835 sentences with a 1 percent noun-frequency floor. A PMI typing pass on this corpus needs a held-out look before any claim (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: The brain shows sentence-level typing gave a higher inverse share (64% vs 41%); it does not show higher accuracy, so rel's 'beat release-level typing' is unsupported. The cfpb_reform +1 and cfpb_expansion -1 values in rel are the intended direction, not constants in code. The 1 percent floor and PMI typing are the paper's steps and are not in Paul's system.

bearings.paper_claim: Direction plus noun carries polarity that a general or finance dictionary misses. LM alone labels 'Profit for the period was EUR 10.9 mn, down from EUR 14.3 mn in 2009' neutral (SentimentScore 0), while the (profit, down) pair gives refined score -1. On DS100, negative-class F1 is 0.4087 for LM alone and 0.7260 for LM+Senti-DD.
bearings.system_side: LSD2015 tone in stage5_lsd.R is a direction-blind count of positive and negative words and negation phrases. Press intensity is |net|/words or charge, multiplied by the DEBATE or human sign, so LSD sets magnitude only and its sign is discarded. For text-less bill rows intensity is a fixed BILL_W (0.03).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. LSD sign is discarded here, so the paper's flips matter for intensity only when directional pairs cancel or inflate |net|, as in cost-cut or fee-reduce releases. The paper tests neither LSD nor intensity, and Paul's system has no human-coded intensity gold to test this against.

The LSD code description checks out (stage5_lsd.R lines 10-15 and 46-58; heat is lsd_charge or abs(lsd_net_norm) in run_stage5.R lines 137-143). The 'magnitude only' point holds for text-bearing rows; text-less rows use the fixed BILL_W.

summary_issues: 'Evaluation covers headline-length sentences only' is wrong: the evaluation sets include 960 SemEval-2017 messages and 436 FiQA sentences; only the construction domain is headline-style (Sect. 3.1).
'Raises weighted F1 ... to 0.71-0.82' holds on the FPB subsets only. The summary omits that Sentiment140, VADER and AFINN beat LM+Senti-DD on SemEval and FiQA.

Omitted validity problem: the lexicon was built from labels on all 4,835 DS50 sentences and scored on DS50 and DS100 with no described fold-wise rebuild. The FPB gains are in-sample for the labels used to build the lexicon, not held-out.

'cfpb_reform +1, cfpb_expansion -1, cfpb_institution 0' is presented as coded values. In derive_valence_registry.py the first two have no hard-coded sign (gold-derived); only cfpb_institution and cfpb_general are fixed at 0, by user-directed policy.

The summary says the paper's failures and class imbalance 'match the churn' in the dry run. The dry run churn came from verb counts over whole release text (3 good / 43 bad), not from lexicon class imbalance; the match is in mechanism only.

The claim that Paul's memory line ('user pursuing a direction-aware sentiment lexicon') is stale is a judgment. The brain records rejection of the override, but the memory file body was not checked for an update.
The item's extraction calls the Table 7 and 8 values layout-garbled. The values parse cleanly once the 13 columns are counted, so the caveat should be dropped or narrowed.
gaps_exposed: No sentence- or headline-scoped direction rule. Every directional-lexicon test in the system counted over whole release text, while the paper's evidence is sentence-level and its pairs require the direction word to govern the noun.

No representation of speaker attitude toward the direction ('defend against efforts to dismantle the CFPB'). The paper does not model this either, and it is the dominant failure mode in Paul's dry run. A direction-pair feature would need dependency or clause scoping before it could help DEBATE.
The direction-pair signal was never tried as a soft feature into the stacked stance readers. That was the recorded pivot option, and it has no held-out measurement.
LSD intensity ignores direction-dependent polarity. Whether this distorts |net| on CU press releases is untested, and there is no human-coded intensity gold.
flags: The system has already tested and rejected this paper's method as adapted: naive directional-verb x target override, 3 good / 43 bad on gold. Do not re-propose a whole-text direction-aware override. Any sentence-scoped revival stays UNVERIFIED until a held-out gold look reproduces it (DE-062).

The paper's F1 values come from layout-garbled table text and have no significance tests or confidence intervals. Check them against the PDF before quoting, and attach the corpus and denominator, e.g. 'weighted F1 on FPB DS100, 2,259 sentences, 5x5-fold CV'.

The paper's domain (European company-performance headlines, mid-2000s to 2010s) is not congressional press. Its evidence does not transfer to the multi-topic releases that dominate the Stage 5 corpus.
paul_alignment: There are no annotations, but Paul acted on the paper. He adapted it for the CFPB sign-flip problem (memory note cu-signflip-directionality; brain two-hop note). The built system agrees with the paper's core idea, that polarity belongs to the pair and not the word: the direction-separated CFPB families in derive_valence_registry.py are a hand-curated Senti-DD. It disagrees on automation, because the automatic and naive version churned (3 good / 43 bad), and the paper's own headline-only scope and class-imbalance warnings predict that. Paul's memory note's present-tense line ('user pursuing a direction-aware sentiment lexicon') is stale. That line of work ended in rejection of the override and the curated registry. The remaining live question is the sentence-scoped or feature-only variant.
